reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Pandas for Real Analytics
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 10. In this module, we are moving from general Python programming into one of the most important tools used in day-to-day data analysis: Pandas.

Pandas helps us work with tabular data, meaning data organized into rows and columns. Think about CSV files, Excel worksheets, database query results, survey data, transaction records, or patient records. These are all common examples of data that can be represented as a Pandas DataFrame.

The goal is not to memorize a long list of commands. Instead, I want you to learn a repeatable workflow. We will load data, inspect it, identify problems, clean those problems, create useful variables, summarize the data, combine tables, and then validate the final result.

[tts-break]

As we move through the module, notice that we will keep asking the same question: can we trust the data we are about to analyze?

By the end of this module, you should be able to take a small messy dataset and turn it into a clean, understandable, and analysis-ready table.

slides.title: Why Pandas matters at work
slides.transcript:
Pandas is important because a large part of analytics work happens before we build a model or create a dashboard.

An analyst may receive a CSV file exported from a business system. A data scientist may receive a table from SQL. A research team may receive data collected from a survey or an experiment. In all of these cases, the data usually needs to be inspected and prepared before it can be used.

Pandas gives us practical tools for this work. We can identify missing values, correct data types, standardize categories, filter rows, calculate summaries, join related tables, and create new variables.

[tts-break]

The professional skill is not simply knowing that a function such as groupby exists. The more valuable skill is being able to look at an unfamiliar dataset and decide what needs to happen next.

For example, if a column called amount contains dollar signs and is stored as text, we need to recognize that before calculating an average. If customer IDs are duplicated unexpectedly, we need to investigate before joining another table.

That kind of reasoning is what makes Pandas useful in real analytical work.

slides.title: What “job-ready Pandas” means
slides.transcript:
When I say job-ready Pandas, I do not mean that you need to memorize every function in the Pandas library.

Pandas is a large library, and even experienced analysts look at the documentation regularly. What matters is being comfortable with the core patterns that appear repeatedly.

You should know how to load data and inspect the rows, columns, data types, missing values, and duplicates. You should be able to select the columns you need, filter rows using business conditions, and sort or rank records.

You should also be comfortable cleaning values, converting data types, standardizing text, working with dates, creating new columns, and summarizing groups.

[tts-break]

Another important skill is combining tables correctly. A merge that looks successful can still be wrong if the relationship between the keys is not what you expected.

Finally, you should validate your work. Check row counts, totals, unique keys, and missing values after major transformations.

The goal is not just to make the code run. The goal is to produce an analytical result that you can explain and defend.

slides.title: The Pandas workflow
slides.transcript:
This slide gives us the workflow we will follow throughout the module.

First, we create or load a DataFrame. In real projects, this may come from a CSV file, an Excel file, a database query, or another application.

Second, we inspect the data. Before changing anything, we need to understand what we received. We look at sample rows, the shape of the table, column names, and data types.

Third, we select the rows and columns that are relevant to our question.

Then we clean the data. This may include fixing types, handling missing values, removing true duplicates, and standardizing text.

[tts-break]

After cleaning, we can transform the data. We might create a profit column, extract the month from a date, or classify transactions into size categories.

Next, we summarize the data using tools such as groupby, agg, pivot_table, and crosstab.

If information is spread across multiple tables, we combine them using merge or concat.

Finally, we validate. We compare row counts, inspect keys, check totals, and make sure our assumptions still hold.

This sequence is useful because it gives structure to an otherwise messy analytical problem.

slides.title: Series and DataFrame
slides.transcript:
Two Pandas objects appear throughout this module: Series and DataFrame.

A Series is essentially one labeled dimension of data. You can think of it as one column together with an index. For example, if we select only the amount column from an orders table, Pandas usually returns a Series.

A DataFrame is a two-dimensional table with rows and columns. Each column has a name, and each column also has a data type.

This distinction matters because some operations behave differently depending on whether you are working with a Series or a DataFrame.

[tts-break]

For example, orders bracket amount returns one column and usually gives us a Series. If we place amount inside a list and use double brackets, Pandas returns a DataFrame containing one column.

This may look like a small difference, but it explains many common beginner errors.

A useful habit is to ask: what kind of object do I have right now? If you are unsure, use type and inspect the result.

Understanding the object you are working with makes the rest of Pandas much easier.

slides.title: Create a DataFrame
slides.transcript:
Now we will create a small DataFrame directly in Python.

In the code, we first import Pandas using the standard alias, pd. Then we pass a list of dictionaries into pd.DataFrame.

Each dictionary represents one row. The dictionary keys become the column names, and the values become the data stored in that row.

Click Run and look at the result.

You should see five order records with order ID, channel, and amount.

[tts-break]

This small example is useful because it lets us practice Pandas without depending on an external file.

Notice that the rows automatically receive an index starting at zero. The index is not the same thing as the order ID. It is Pandas' label for the rows unless we explicitly change it.

Try changing one amount or adding another order to the list, then run the code again.

The point of this slide is not the specific numbers. It is to understand how a collection of Python records becomes a structured DataFrame that we can inspect and analyze.

slides.title: Load CSV data
slides.transcript:
Most of the time, we will not type our data directly into Python. We will load it from somewhere.

One of the most common formats is CSV, which stands for comma-separated values.

In this example, we create CSV text inside Python and then use StringIO so Pandas can treat that text like a small file. The important function is pd.read_csv.

Click Run.

Pandas reads the header row and uses those values as column names. Each later line becomes one row in the DataFrame.

We also print the type of the result, and you should see that it is a Pandas DataFrame.

[tts-break]

In real work, the syntax may be as simple as pd.read_csv followed by the filename.

The same general idea applies when data comes from SQL. SQL may retrieve the rows, and Pandas becomes the environment where we inspect, clean, transform, and summarize those rows.

A good practice is to never assume that a file loaded perfectly. Loading is only the first step. The next step should always be inspection.

slides.title: First inspection: rows and shape
slides.transcript:
Before analyzing a new dataset, inspect it.

In this example, we use several simple tools that should become automatic habits.

Head shows the first few rows. This helps us understand the general structure and whether the values look reasonable.

Shape gives us two numbers: the number of rows and the number of columns.

Columns gives us the column names.

Sample returns a few randomly selected rows. Here we set random_state so the same sample appears each time.

Click Run and look at each output separately.

[tts-break]

Imagine receiving a file that someone tells you contains ten thousand records. If shape shows only nine hundred rows, that is something we should investigate immediately.

The same idea applies after cleaning. If we start with one thousand rows and end with six hundred, we need to understand why four hundred rows disappeared.

A simple row count can detect serious analytical problems.

So one of the most important habits in this module is this: know the size and basic structure of your data before and after major transformations.

slides.title: Inspect dtypes and structure
slides.transcript:
Data can look correct on the screen and still be stored incorrectly.

In this example, order date looks like a date, and amount looks like a number. But both columns are initially stored as text.

Click Run and look at the dtypes output.

You will see that Pandas does not automatically know that these strings should be interpreted as dates or numeric values.

Then look at info. The info method gives us a compact summary of the DataFrame, including column names, non-null counts, data types, and memory information.

[tts-break]

Why does this matter?

If amount is stored as text, numerical operations may fail or produce unexpected behavior. If order date is stored as text, we cannot easily extract the month, weekday, or time difference.

This is why checking data types is part of data quality work.

Do not decide what a column is based only on how it looks. Ask Pandas what type it is actually using.

Later in the module, we will convert these values safely.

slides.title: Summaries and category counts
slides.transcript:
Once we understand the basic structure, we can begin a quick exploratory analysis.

The describe method summarizes numerical columns. It can show the count, mean, standard deviation, minimum, quartiles, and maximum.

Value_counts is especially useful for categorical data. It tells us how often each category appears.

Nunique tells us how many distinct values exist.

Click Run and inspect the output.

[tts-break]

These simple functions can reveal problems very quickly.

For example, suppose a channel column is expected to contain web, email, and store. If value_counts returns Web, web, WEB, and web with spaces as separate categories, we probably have a text-cleaning issue.

For numeric data, describe can reveal suspicious ranges. If an age column has a minimum of negative five or a maximum of nine hundred, we need to investigate.

EDA does not begin with complicated charts. Often it begins with simple counts, ranges, and questions about whether the values make sense in the real-world context.

slides.title: Select columns
slides.transcript:
Analytical datasets often contain more columns than we need for a specific task.

In this example, we select one column and then two columns.

When we use one set of brackets with a single column name, Pandas usually returns a Series.

When we use a list of column names inside double brackets, Pandas returns a DataFrame.

Click Run and compare the outputs.

[tts-break]

Selecting only the variables you need can make an analysis easier to understand.

Imagine a dataset with fifty columns, but your question only involves customer segment, order amount, and date. Keeping those three columns visible can reduce confusion while you develop the analysis.

This also helps when sharing results with someone else. A small, focused table is often easier to review than a very wide DataFrame.

Remember the key idea: one column selected directly usually gives you a Series. A list of columns gives you a DataFrame.

slides.title: Use loc and iloc
slides.transcript:
Pandas gives us two important selection tools: loc and iloc.

Loc is label-based. We normally use column names and, when needed, row labels or Boolean conditions.

Iloc is position-based. It uses integer positions.

In the first example, loc finds rows where channel equals web, then returns the order ID and amount columns.

In the second example, iloc selects rows zero through one and columns zero through one using positions.

Click Run and compare the results.

[tts-break]

For analytical code, loc is often easier to read because the code tells us what the columns mean.

For example, selecting order ID and amount is much clearer to a future reader than selecting columns zero and two.

Iloc is still useful when position itself matters, such as selecting the first few columns or working with a known table structure.

The important distinction is simple: loc means labels and conditions; iloc means integer positions.

slides.title: Filter rows with conditions
slides.transcript:
Filtering is how we turn a business question into a subset of rows.

In this example, the first question is: which web orders have an amount of at least one hundred?

We create two conditions and combine them using the ampersand operator, which means AND.

Notice the parentheses around each condition. In Pandas, those parentheses are important when combining Boolean expressions.

The second example uses query to find all orders with amount greater than or equal to one hundred.

Click Run and compare the two results.

[tts-break]

Filtering should always connect to a meaningful question.

Instead of thinking, I need to practice greater-than syntax, think: which transactions exceed our review threshold? Which patients are older than sixty-five? Which products had sales below target?

That change in thinking matters because the syntax becomes attached to a real analytical purpose.

Also remember that a filter changes which rows are included. Before continuing, it is often useful to check how many rows remain.

slides.title: Sort and find top records
slides.transcript:
Sorting helps us prioritize records and understand extremes.

In this example, sort_values orders the DataFrame by amount from largest to smallest.

Then nlargest returns the three rows with the largest amount values.

Click Run and compare the two outputs.

Sort_values keeps all rows but changes their order. Nlargest is useful when you only want the top few records.

[tts-break]

This pattern appears often in real work.

You may want the highest-revenue products, the customers with the largest balances, the departments with the most incidents, or the top-performing campaigns.

The opposite function, nsmallest, can help identify the lowest values.

One caution: top values are not automatically the most important values. A large transaction may be valid, or it may be an outlier or data-entry error.

Sorting helps you find what deserves attention. Interpretation still requires context.

slides.title: A messy dataset is normal
slides.transcript:
Now we move into the cleaning section.

This table is intentionally messy because real data frequently contains small inconsistencies that can create large analytical problems.

Look at the channel column. We have values such as Web, EMAIL, web, and Store with inconsistent capitalization and spacing.

The amount column contains currency symbols and also a missing value.

One date is not a valid date.

The city column has a missing value.

And order ID one thousand three appears twice.

[tts-break]

None of these problems is unusual.

The danger is that some of them are easy to miss. A duplicate can inflate revenue. Inconsistent categories can split one group into several fake groups. A bad date can break time-based analysis.

Our goal is not to immediately start deleting or filling values.

First we need to measure the problems and understand what each one means.

Good data cleaning is not a sequence of automatic commands. It is a sequence of decisions supported by evidence.

slides.title: Profile data quality
slides.transcript:
Before changing messy data, profile it.

This code loads the sample sales data and then checks three important areas: missing values, duplicate rows, and data types.

Click Run.

The isna method identifies missing values, and sum counts them by column.

Duplicated identifies rows that repeat exactly.

Dtypes shows how Pandas currently stores each column.

[tts-break]

This step creates a baseline.

For example, if we know there are two missing values before cleaning, we can verify later whether our cleaning strategy handled them.

If we remove duplicates, we can compare the number of rows before and after.

This is especially important in professional work because cleaning should be explainable.

Instead of saying, I cleaned the file, we should be able to say, the original file had five rows, one exact duplicate, one missing amount, one missing city, and one invalid date.

That kind of description makes the workflow reproducible and easier to review.

slides.title: Convert types safely
slides.transcript:
Now we will convert two columns that are currently stored as text.

The amount column contains dollar signs. Before converting it to a number, we remove the dollar sign using a vectorized string operation.

Then pd.to_numeric converts the cleaned strings into numeric values.

Notice errors equals coerce.

Coerce means that if Pandas encounters a value that cannot be converted, it replaces that value with a missing value rather than crashing the whole operation.

We use the same idea with pd.to_datetime.

Click Run and inspect both the values and the resulting data types.

[tts-break]

This is a safer analytical pattern because invalid data becomes visible.

For example, the text not-a-date becomes a missing datetime value. That tells us we have a quality problem that still needs a decision.

We are not pretending that the invalid date is correct.

A useful principle is: convert first, then inspect what became missing. Conversion is not the end of cleaning; it often reveals the next problem we need to handle.

slides.title: Handle missing values deliberately
slides.transcript:
Missing values require reasoning.

There is no single correct command that works for every situation.

In this example, the city column contains one missing value. We replace that value with the label Unknown.

For amount, we demonstrate filling the missing value with the median.

Click Run and compare the missing-value counts before and after.

[tts-break]

The important lesson is not that median is always the correct answer. It is only a teaching example.

Imagine that amount is missing because the transaction was cancelled. Filling it with the median might create a false transaction value.

In another dataset, a missing city may mean the customer refused to provide a location. Replacing it with Unknown may be appropriate because the missingness itself has meaning.

Other choices include dropping the row, leaving the value missing, using a business rule, or creating a separate indicator showing that the original value was missing.

Always ask why the value is missing before deciding how to handle it.

slides.title: Find and remove duplicates
slides.transcript:
Duplicates can distort an analysis, but we must define what duplicate means.

In this example, order ID is treated as the business key. That means we expect one row per order.

We use duplicated with subset equal to order ID and keep equals false to display every record involved in a duplicate.

Then drop_duplicates keeps the first record for each repeated order ID.

Click Run and inspect the output.

[tts-break]

Now consider an important real-world question.

What if the table represents order line items instead of orders?

One order ID could legitimately appear several times because the customer purchased several products.

In that case, removing repeated order IDs would destroy valid data.

This is why row grain matters. Grain means what one row represents.

Before removing duplicates, state the grain explicitly. One row per order? One row per customer? One row per product within an order?

Duplicate removal is only correct when it respects the meaning of the row.

slides.title: Clean text columns
slides.transcript:
Small text differences can create fake categories.

In this example, the channel column contains values such as Web with spaces, EMAIL in uppercase, web in lowercase, and Store with spaces.

The status column has the same problem.

We use the string accessor, str, to apply text methods to the entire column.

Strip removes leading and trailing spaces.

Lower converts the text to lowercase.

Click Run and then look at value_counts for channel.

[tts-break]

Before cleaning, values that mean the same thing could be counted separately.

After cleaning, Web, web, and values with extra spaces become one consistent category.

This matters for groupby, pivot tables, charts, and machine-learning features.

Be careful, however, not to standardize blindly. Sometimes capitalization or spacing is meaningful.

The goal is to create consistent categories based on the meaning of the data, not simply to modify text because a method is available.

slides.title: Create derived columns
slides.transcript:
A major strength of Pandas is vectorized column operations.

Here we create several new variables from the existing amount column.

First, tax is calculated as amount multiplied by seven percent.

Then total with tax is amount plus tax.

Finally, pd.cut places each order into a size category: small, medium, or large.

Click Run and inspect the new columns.

[tts-break]

Notice that we do not write a loop that processes one row at a time.

We describe the calculation once, and Pandas applies it across the entire column.

This style is usually clearer and more efficient.

Derived columns are common in analytics.

You may calculate profit from revenue and cost, length of stay from two dates, age from birth date, response time from timestamps, or customer category from spending thresholds.

When you create a derived column, document the business rule. Someone should be able to understand exactly how that value was produced.

slides.title: Work with dates
slides.transcript:
Dates become much more useful after they are converted to a real datetime type.

In this example, the order_date column is already converted using pd.to_datetime.

Then we use the dt accessor.

Dt.month_name returns the month name.

Dt.day_name returns the weekday.

Dt.quarter returns the quarter number.

Click Run and inspect the new columns.

[tts-break]

These features can support many analytical questions.

Do sales change by weekday? Are there seasonal patterns? Which quarter had the most transactions? Are hospital admissions higher during certain months?

We can also calculate differences between dates, extract the year, or group records by time periods.

The key lesson is that a date stored as text is limited. A true datetime value gives us access to time-based operations.

Before using a date in analysis, confirm that it was parsed successfully and check for invalid values that became missing.

slides.title: GroupBy: answer questions by category
slides.transcript:
GroupBy is one of the most important patterns in Pandas.

A useful way to understand it is split, apply, combine.

First, Pandas splits the rows into groups based on a category.

Then it applies a calculation within each group.

Finally, it combines the results into a summary.

In this example, we group by channel and sum the amount column.

Click Run.

The result tells us total revenue for web, email, and store.

[tts-break]

Now connect that code to a business question: which channel contributes the most revenue?

That is the important part. GroupBy is not just syntax; it is a way to answer questions at a different level of detail.

The original table has one row per order. The grouped result has one row or value per channel.

Whenever you group data, ask what one output row represents.

This is the same concept of grain that we discussed during duplicate handling.

slides.title: Aggregate multiple metrics
slides.transcript:
Often one summary measure is not enough.

We may want to know the number of orders, total revenue, and average order value for each channel.

The agg method lets us calculate several measures in one grouped analysis.

In this example, we group by channel and use named aggregation.

Orders counts the number of records.

Revenue sums the amount.

Average order calculates the mean.

Click Run and look at the result.

[tts-break]

Named aggregation is especially useful because the output columns already have meaningful names.

This is much easier to use in a report or dashboard than columns with confusing multi-level labels.

Also notice as_index equals false. This keeps channel as a regular column rather than moving it into the index.

When building summaries, think about the measures that answer the question. More metrics are not automatically better. Choose metrics that help someone understand the behavior of each group.

slides.title: Pivot tables and crosstabs
slides.transcript:
Pivot tables and crosstabs are useful when we want to compare two categorical dimensions.

In the first example, pivot_table summarizes amount by channel and status.

Rows represent channels. Columns represent status values. The cells contain summed revenue.

Fill_value equals zero makes empty combinations easier to interpret.

Then crosstab counts how many records occur for each channel and status combination.

Click Run and compare the two tables.

[tts-break]

Think of pivot_table as similar to an Excel pivot table. It is useful when you want a compact matrix-style summary.

Crosstab is especially convenient when you want counts of category combinations.

For example, you could compare department by diagnosis, product type by region, or survey response by demographic group.

The important question is what the cell means. Is it a count, a sum, an average, or another statistic?

Always make the meaning of the table clear.

slides.title: Merge related tables
slides.transcript:
Real analytical projects often require information from more than one table.

In this example, the orders table has customer IDs but does not have the customer segment.

The customers table contains customer ID and segment.

We use merge to bring the segment information into the order table.

The key is customer_id.

We use a left join because we want to keep every order, even if a customer record is missing.

Click Run and inspect the merged result.

[tts-break]

The validate argument is very important.

Many-to-one tells Pandas that many orders may belong to one customer, but each customer ID should appear only once in the customer table.

If that assumption is violated, Pandas can raise an error instead of silently multiplying rows.

After any merge, check the row count and look for unmatched keys.

A join can run without errors and still be logically wrong. Validation protects us from that kind of silent analytical mistake.

slides.title: Concatenate similar tables
slides.transcript:
Merge combines tables using a key. Concat does something different.

Concat is commonly used when tables have the same or compatible columns and we want to stack them together.

In this example, we have January orders and February orders.

Both tables contain order ID, month, and amount.

Pd.concat stacks the February rows underneath the January rows.

Ignore_index equals true creates a fresh continuous index.

Click Run and inspect the combined table.

[tts-break]

This is a common workflow when data arrives as separate monthly files, regional files, or batches.

Before concatenating many files, check that the columns have compatible meanings and data types.

For example, one file may call a column amount while another calls it sales_amount. One month may store numbers as numeric values while another stores them as text.

Concat is simple, but the consistency of the source tables still matters.

slides.title: Prefer vectorized operations
slides.transcript:
Pandas is designed to work efficiently with whole columns.

In this example, margin is calculated by dividing the profit column by the sales column.

This is a vectorized operation.

We then use map with a small lambda function only to format the margin for display as a percentage.

Click Run and inspect both columns.

[tts-break]

A common beginner habit is to write a Python loop or a row-wise apply for every calculation.

Sometimes custom functions are necessary, but built-in Pandas operations are usually clearer and often faster.

For example, if you can express the task as one column plus another column, or as a string method, comparison, arithmetic operation, or datetime operation, prefer that approach.

Think in columns whenever possible.

This becomes increasingly important as datasets grow because row-by-row Python logic can become a performance bottleneck.

slides.title: End-to-end cleaning workflow
slides.transcript:
Now we will combine several ideas into one small workflow.

The input is a messy sales extract.

First, we remove duplicate order IDs and create a copy.

Then we standardize channel and status using strip and lower.

Next, we clean the amount column by removing the dollar sign and converting the result to numeric values.

We convert the date column to datetime and coerce invalid dates to missing values.

Then we fill the missing city with Unknown and fill the missing amount using the median for this teaching example.

Click Run and inspect the final DataFrame.

[tts-break]

The important lesson is the order of operations.

We are not randomly applying Pandas functions. We are following a sequence that we can explain.

Profile the data, understand the problems, convert types, standardize categories, handle missingness, remove true duplicates, and then inspect the result.

In a production project, each decision would need to be justified more carefully, but this gives you a practical starting pattern.

slides.title: Analyze and validate the cleaned data
slides.transcript:
Cleaning is not finished when the code stops producing errors.

We need to verify the result.

This example starts with a cleaned DataFrame and performs several checks.

We print the number of rows.

We count duplicated order IDs.

We count the total number of missing values.

Then we keep only completed orders and summarize them by channel.

Finally, we calculate total revenue as another check.

Click Run and inspect each part.

[tts-break]

Validation should answer questions such as: did we accidentally duplicate records? Did we remove more rows than expected? Are required fields still missing? Does the grouped revenue equal the total revenue from the filtered table?

These checks can catch errors before the data is used in a dashboard, statistical analysis, or machine-learning model.

A professional notebook should not only produce results. It should contain evidence that the results are based on data that still follows the assumptions of the analysis.

slides.title: A compact analyst workflow
slides.transcript:
This slide summarizes the entire module into one practical sequence.

Load the data.

Profile it using head, shape, info, missing-value counts, and duplicate checks.

Clean the important problems using tools such as to_numeric, fillna, drop_duplicates, and string methods.

Select the rows and columns relevant to the question.

Create useful transformations, including derived columns and date features.

Summarize using groupby, agg, and pivot tables.

Combine related sources using merge or concat.

Then validate row counts, keys, missing values, and totals.

[tts-break]

If you remember this workflow, you do not need to memorize hundreds of Pandas functions.

You can use documentation when you need a specific method.

Also remember that Pandas is not always the best tool for every dataset.

If the data is extremely large, it may be more appropriate to perform part of the work in SQL, Spark, Pollars, or another system.

Knowing when to use Pandas and when not to use Pandas is also part of professional analytical judgment.

slides.title: Module 10 practice challenge
slides.transcript:
Now it is your turn to apply the workflow independently.

Start by creating a DataFrame with at least eight rows or loading a small CSV file.

Then inspect it. Show the first rows, the shape, the data types, missing values, and duplicates.

Next, identify at least one issue that needs cleaning. It could be a data type, a text category, a missing value, or a duplicate.

After cleaning, create at least one useful derived column.

Then use groupby or pivot_table to answer a question about the data.

[tts-break]

Do not stop when the code runs.

Write two sentences explaining what your result means.

Then write one limitation.

For example, you might say that one category has the highest average value, but the dataset is small or covers only one month.

There is no single required solution for this exercise. The goal is to demonstrate that you can make reasonable analytical decisions and explain why you made them.

slides.title: Job-ready Pandas checklist
slides.transcript:
This checklist summarizes the Pandas skills I want you to keep practicing.

For core table work, be comfortable with DataFrame, Series, read_csv, head, shape, dtypes, and info.

For selection, practice column selection, loc, iloc, Boolean masks, query, and sorting.

For cleaning, know how to identify missing values and duplicates, convert types safely, work with strings, and make deliberate decisions about missing data.

For analysis, practice describe, value_counts, groupby, agg, pivot_table, and crosstab.

For combining data, understand merge, concat, join relationships, and validation.

[tts-break]

And do not forget the professional habits behind the syntax.

Use vectorized operations when possible.

Verify assumptions after major transformations.

Document important cleaning decisions.

Check row counts and keys after joins.

And know when the data may be better handled in SQL or a larger-scale system.

If you are comfortable with these patterns, you have a strong foundation for practical Pandas work.

slides.title: References and next steps
slides.transcript:
This final slide gives you resources for continuing your Pandas learning.

The official Pandas documentation should become a normal part of your workflow. You do not need to memorize every parameter. Learn the core patterns, and then use the documentation when you need details.

The Pandas user guide and the introductory tutorials are especially useful because they provide examples for selection, missing data, grouping, merging, reshaping, and many other common tasks.

[tts-break]

Your best next step is practice.

Choose a small real CSV dataset and begin with a question, not with code.

Write down what you want to learn from the data.

Then load the file, inspect it, identify quality problems, clean only what needs to be cleaned, create useful transformations, summarize the result, and validate what you produced.

That process is more valuable than memorizing a long list of functions.

In the next module, we can build on this foundation with more advanced Pandas workflows, reshaping, time-series analysis, and performance-oriented techniques.
